To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in consecutive screening samples from Belgian women, any of the genital HPV (sub‐)types was found at a high prevalence (37.1%); Hr‐HPVs were detected more frequently than Lr‐HPVs and the six possibly Hr‐HPVS (26.8 vs. 16.4 and 6.6%, respectively); high viral loads of HPV were detected in 17.1% of the screening samples; among women with cytological abnormality, the frequency

the prevalence of Hr and L‐rHPV types in a screening population of Belgian women was 26.8% and 16.4% respectively, and that the prevalence of high‐risk HPV types increased from 5.3% in the negative cytology group to 47.1% in LSIL and to 91.8% in HSIL.
the prevalence of 54 genital HPV types was high in a screening population, and that the prevalence of high‐risk (Hr‐) HPV infections increased with increasing cytological abnormalities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the epidemiology of genital HPV types and the relationship of HPV‐DNA load with cervical cytology in a Belgian screening cohort.
the prevalence, viral loads and type‐specific differences of 51 genital HPV (sub‐)types in consecutive cervical screening samples.

the prevalence and viral loads of 51 genital HPV (subtypes) in consecutive screening samples and a representative set of abnormal cytology samples from women attending routine gynecological check‐ups.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the majority of the 54 HPV types and three HPV subtypes are not equally prevalent and that their prevalence and viral load differ considerably between cytological groups.
the prevalence of HPV in the screening population is high (37.1%), and the majority of HPV infections are of low viral load (80.3%).
the prevalence and viral loads of Hrviruses in cervical samples from women with ASC‐US and LSIL are higher than in those with HSIL.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the majority of the HPV‐positive women in the general population had low viral loads of Lr‐HPVs, while the majority of the women with cytologic abnormalities had high viral loads of high‐risk HPV types.
the prevalence of Hr‐ and Lr‐types is high in the general population, but that high viral loads are more common in women with cytological HSIL.
Hr‐HPVs are more prevalent and have a higher viral load in abnormal cervical samples than in normal ones and that the viral load of Hr‐ and Lr‐types differs substantially among individual types.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distinction between Hr‐ and Lr‐types is not as clear‐cut as is generally thought, and that high viral load is not a good predictor for progression of Hr‐type infections.
the prevalence of Hr‐ and Lr‐types is similar in screening samples and that high viral load infections are more common than expected.
high‐grade cervical disease can develop without high viral load Hr‐HPVs.
